name: Scoro
subcategory: agency work management (quotes, time, invoicing, reporting)
tagline: All-in-one work management for agencies and consultancies: quotes, projects, time tracking, invoicing and profitability reports in one place.

pricing.basis: per user per month, seat minimum applies
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Scoro is not one clever feature, it is five boring ones stapled together: quote, plan, log time, invoice, then show whether the job made money. Each of those is a CRUD table, and an agent can wire the whole chain into a local app over a weekend, which is genuinely useful if you are a solo consultant who currently does this in three spreadsheets. What does not survive is the half of Scoro that talks to other systems: accounting sync, calendar and email two-way, seat permissions, mobile timers, and reports your accountant will accept without argument. The moat is breadth plus plumbing, not secret sauce. Build it if you are one person billing hours; do not build it if five people need to agree on the same numbers.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you create a quote, turn it into a project with tasks and a budget, log time against it, generate an invoice PDF, and see margin per client and per project.
requirements: a PDF library for invoice output
optional: your own tax rates and invoice numbering rules
whatYouLose: Accounting integrations: no Xero or QuickBooks sync, so invoices get re-entered by hand somewhere
Two-way calendar and email sync, which is where a lot of Scoro's daily convenience actually lives
Multi-user roles, approvals and the shared source of truth that makes a team stop arguing about hours
Mobile apps and a phone timer, so time logged away from the laptop is reconstructed from memory
Resource planning, utilization forecasting and the report polish you would show a client or a bank
moatNotes: Years of quotes, timesheets and invoices in one schema is the real lock-in. Nobody migrates billing history for fun.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the thing being replaced is not software, it is agreement. Once more than one person bills time, the value is that everyone logs into the same system, the numbers reconcile with the accounting package, and the invoice that goes out is the invoice the report counted. Paying per seat buys you the boring guarantees: audit trail, permissions, exports your bookkeeper accepts, and someone else's problem when the VAT logic changes. A solo operator can absolutely live in a homemade version, and many do, right up until they hire the second person.
notes: Great weekend build for a one-person consultancy, mediocre substitute the moment payroll exists.
prompt:
Build a local-first work management app for a solo consultant. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Zod for validation, pdf-lib for PDF output. Single user, no auth, runs on localhost with `npm run dev`. Database file at ./data/app.db, created and migrated on first boot with plain SQL migrations, no ORM.

Data model: clients, quotes, quote_lines, projects, tasks, time_entries, invoices, invoice_lines, expenses, settings.

Core flow to implement end to end:
1. Create a client with billing address, default hourly rate, currency and tax rate.
2. Create a quote for a client with line items (description, quantity, unit price). Show subtotal, tax, total. Statuses: draft, sent, accepted, lost.
3. One click converts an accepted quote into a project: copies lines into tasks, sets a budget in money and hours.
4. Log time against a task: date, minutes, billable flag, note. Include a start/stop timer that survives a page reload by storing the running entry in the database.
5. Generate an invoice from unbilled billable time plus selected expenses on a project. Sequential invoice numbers from settings, editable lines, statuses: draft, sent, paid. Export to PDF with pdf-lib using company details from settings.
6. Dashboard: this month billable hours, unbilled value, overdue invoices, and a per project table showing budget vs logged hours vs invoiced vs margin.

Also include: CSV export for time_entries and invoices, a JSON backup and restore of the whole database, and seed data behind `npm run seed`.

Explicitly out of scope: multi-user and permissions, accounting or calendar or email integrations, payment collection, recurring billing, mobile app, notifications.

Keep the UI plain: sidebar nav, dense tables, keyboard-friendly forms, no charting library. Put company name, address, tax number and invoice prefix in .env.example and read them into settings on first run. Write a README with setup, the data model, and a one paragraph list of what this deliberately does not do.
